cards.title: TaskLens: Generating Task-Conditioned Scaffolded Interfaces for Learning Professional Creative Software

rows.value: other
framework or design space, design principle, primary empirical, failure or counterevidence, measurement or method

TaskLens is explicitly grounded in instructional scaffolding and combines task-centric interfaces, adaptive UI configuration, training-wheels-style progressive disclosure, novice-to-expert transition guidance, cognitive-load concerns, and learning by doing. Several traditions directly shape implemented interface features, while NASA-TLX and ARCS-informed custom measures shape evaluation. The grounding is therefore mixed between conceptual use and operationalization; durable transfer to native-interface fluency remains proposed rather than longitudinally tested.

medium · The design pattern and immediate novice effects are directly supported, but individual scaffold components were not isolated. Generalization is limited by 32 beginners completing two short Blender tasks, several custom self-report measures, and an eight-person qualitative expert study. Long-term transfer, scaffold fading, open-ended creative work, and cross-software effectiveness were not directly evaluated.

cards.title: When Scaffolding Breaks: Investigating Student Interaction with LLM-Based Writing Support in Real-Time K-12 EFL Classrooms

rows.value: other
primary empirical, failure or counterevidence, design principle, framework or design space

A six-week deployment of an LLM writing assistant in a real South Korean middle school, and one of the few papers in this corpus whose subject is a support failing. Van de Pol's six scaffolding strategies were written straight into the system prompt, with an explicit instruction not to give the answer at once, and 157 eighth-graders used the result across two writing units. The finding the review needs is the split between what happened under the tool and what survived it. In class the sentences built with the assistant were grammatically sound for everyone, most of all for the weakest students at 86.2%. Two to three weeks later, writing the same essay with no teacher and no AI, high performers carried 65.8% of those sentences correctly into their own work and low performers 14.0%. Alongside that, frustration ran roughly three times higher in the lower groups and piled up in the second half of each period, because a hint-only design costs time a student in a 45-minute lesson does not control. The authors therefore argue against the field's own non-disclosure norm. The classroom effects are as consequential: four or five students of 26 kept the teacher's attention, quiet students asked less than before, peer questions went to the machine, and the recurring questions the teacher used to diagnose the room stopped arriving. No control condition, groups cut from the outcome score itself, and correctness judged by GPT-4o.

medium · The core comparison is unusually well placed: the same sentences are scored under the tool and, two to three weeks later, in an essay written with no teacher and no AI. That the transfer gap runs 65.8, 37.8 and 14.0 down the proficiency scale while in-class accuracy did not is hard to explain away. What weakens the size of every group number is the same three things. There is no control condition and no pre-test, so nothing compares these students against no tool or a direct-answer tool. The performance groups are cut from the score on the very assessment the transfer is measured in, which is circular. And grammatical correctness was judged by GPT-4o on the strength of one cited preprint. The qualitative and classroom findings rest on fifteen coded students, three observed sessions and one teacher who also co-designed the system; students were never asked anything, by design. Directions are solid, magnitudes are not.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: The paper's most useful result, and the reason it belongs in this review: the support did not fail while it was present, it failed on removal, and it failed hardest for the students it was built for. Under the tool the low-performing group's sentences were the most grammatically accurate of any group, 86.2%. Two to three weeks later, writing the same-topic essay alone with no teacher and no AI, that group carried 14.0% of those sentences correctly into their own work, against 37.8% for the middle group and 65.8% for the high group. An in-class artifact gap of nothing became a post-removal gap of nearly five to one. Two things bound the claim and neither is small. What is measured is whether an LLM-built sentence reappeared correctly in the later essay, which is reuse, not knowledge: a student who wrote something different or better scores as a non-transfer, and the paper does not separate those cases. And the groups are defined by the score on that same later assessment, so the split is partly circular. The denominators behind 65.8, 37.8 and 14.0 are not printed, the analysis covers one semester and one feature, and grammatical correctness was judged by GPT-4o rather than a person.

rows.value: During the fall semester, students constructed a total of 632 sentences with the assistance of an LLM. Of these, 309 sentences (48.9% of the total) were incorporated verbatim into the students' final essays, with 82.3% of them being grammatically correct. This trend was also observed in the low-performing group, where 86.2% of the sentences constructed with the LLM were grammatically accurate. However, while students in the high-performing group correctly incorporated 65.8% of these sentences into their final written assessments, students in the middle- and low-performing groups only did so 37.8% and 14.0% of the time, respectively. These findings suggest that, regardless of proficiency level, the use of an LLM can serve as an effective tool for improving students' grammatical accuracy during in-class activities. However, the degree to which students retain and appropriately transfer these sentences into their final written work appears to differ across performance groups.

items.lead: This is the mechanism behind the title, and the authors argue directly against a norm their own field holds. Confusion and annoyance ran at 3.8 per writing session for high performers against 12.2 and 11.4 for middle and low, roughly threefold. The causes differed in kind, not just in rate: high performers were annoyed when the model missed their intent, one of them by getting an indirect hint instead of a straight answer to 'What is a peak in English?'; low performers were annoyed by the step-by-step feedback itself, most often answering 'I don't know' over and over while the model kept guiding. Figure 4 prints that spiral ending in 'I SAID I DON'T KNOW!!!'. The timing is the diagnostic part: 69.2% of the lower groups' negative affect fell in the second half of a session, against an even 52.5% for high performers, which is what an accumulating cost looks like rather than a bad first impression. The condition the authors name is not proficiency alone but proficiency plus motivation plus a fixed period the student cannot extend. Non-disclosure spends the learner's time to buy learning; in a timed lesson that is a resource the learner does not control. Worth noting that the prompt already contained a fallback, to give the answer with explanations if a student continuously struggles, so what broke was not a strawman design.

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: The scaffold did not merely fail to help, it manufactured wrong English, and the three causes the paper gives are all about the fit between the model and its setting rather than about model quality. First, first-language interference: students wrote Korean-shaped input with subjects or predicates dropped, which is normal in Korean and not allowed in English, and the model misread the intent and returned sentences that were grammatically wrong or meant something else. Second, word order: a student wrote 'Many people visit this place and Korean I want' in Korean, and instead of restructuring the sentence the model translated it element by element starting from 'Many'. Third, and sharpest, the classroom's own constraint. The unit required an object relative pronoun; students asked the system to force it in where it did not belong; the system complied, turning 'I want to introduce Poeun art hole' into 'I want to introduce a place that is Poeun art hole', rather than saying the request was wrong. A support that cannot decline an instruction inherits every bad constraint in the lesson plan. There is a design irony underneath: the very feature that let beginners express themselves, code-mixed Korean-English input used in 31.84% of queries, is the feature that fed the model the input it misread.

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: An effect on the classroom rather than on the individual, and it is a redistribution rather than a loss. Teacher attention is fixed; four or five students of 26 already claimed most of it in every observed session; adding an always-available and less intimidating alternative did not spread that attention, it removed the quiet students' remaining reason to compete for it. The tool's approachability is the mechanism, which is uncomfortable because approachability is exactly what it was designed for, and the literature the authors cite says LLMs help shy students. Alongside it, peer learning fell: questions previously put to more proficient classmates now went to the machine, which the authors say increased access to question-asking while reducing collaborative learning, and which they name plainly as efficiency bought at the cost of peer learning. There was a counter-current worth keeping: students did compare LLM outputs with each other and shared moments like 'It gave me a compliment!', so a new kind of peer interaction appeared even as the old kind thinned. The evidence is field notes across three 45-minute sessions plus one follow-up interview with the single participating teacher, with no before-and-after count of who asked what, so the direction is well supported and the size is not.

items.heading: Claim 6 · CLAIM-006
items.lead: The most structural of the paper's failures, and the one most likely to recur wherever an assistant is dropped into a classroom. The teacher was running a live sampler: recurring questions told her which concept to stop and reteach the whole room. The assistant did not destroy that signal, it moved it into a log nobody was reading during the lesson. The abstract puts the consequence more bluntly than the results section does, saying the system's assistance made it difficult for teachers to identify struggling students, and the conclusion adds that struggling students' difficulties were masked by AI-polished outputs. So there are two distinct losses here: the diagnostic signal from questions, and the diagnostic signal from the work itself, since a weak student's essay now looks like a strong one. This is why the authors' own remedy is a real-time teacher-facing dashboard of common errors, progress and engagement, and why they frame it as an equity measure rather than a convenience: without it the teacher's picture of the room is set by the four or five students who still ask aloud. None of this is measured. It comes from observation and the teacher's account, and no attempt was made to test whether a dashboard would restore the signal.

items.heading: Claim 8 · CLAIM-008
items.lead: A clean, fully documented case of an education-research scaffolding taxonomy being translated straight into computational form, which makes it useful for the lineage question quite apart from its findings. Van de Pol, Volman and Beishuizen's six strategies, feeding back, hints, instructing, explaining, modeling and questioning, were not used to evaluate the system afterwards; they were pasted into the system prompt as an enumerated menu, and the model was told to read the transcript, pick the fitting strategy and generate the next teacher turn from it. Table 1 prints what each looked like in production. Two features of the translation are worth recording. Contingency, the part that makes scaffolding scaffolding, is delegated entirely to the model's read of the conversation, with no diagnosis of the learner beyond the transcript. And fading, the third classic function, is absent from the menu: nothing in the design withdraws support as competence grows, and support is instead withdrawn all at once when the assessment arrives weeks later. Around the prompt sit three other design choices worth carrying: four labelled tabs rather than one open chat, because open-ended interfaces overwhelm students with low AI literacy; Korean or code-mixed input allowed on purpose; and a fallback instruction to give the answer with explanations if the student continuously struggles.
